proves: beat is the explainability payoff and the reason candidates are kept on the entry. ID means Identifier is a claim; ID means Identifier and the catalog had also seen seven other long forms is a decision a reviewer can check.
An empty beat is how a token that was never ambiguous is told apart from one whose ambiguity was resolved. Both yield one long form and only one of them was a choice.
A scored resolution reports SCORED, never GOVERNED. The catalog carried the collision and nobody ruled on it, so the answer is a published rule of thumb and the audit trail says so.

Register and Regional both cost eight and neither trips a morphology rule, so the score cannot separate them and the lexicographic tie-break does. The answer is defensible only as a deterministic rule, which is the argument for recording a pin.
The lowest confidence in the corpus. A consumer filtering on an exact 1.0 is asking to see only what the standard confirms, and that filter is worth nothing if an unconfirmed row claims a full score.
An abbreviation read two ways in the wild carries lower confidence than its neighbours, so the audit trail grades unconfirmed rows against each other rather than lumping them together.
An allow-list member has no catalog row, so entry_id is null rather than an invented handle. The audit trail declines to claim a provenance that does not exist.
A passthrough beats nothing, cites nothing and claims nothing. Zero confidence here is the absence of an answer, not low confidence in one.
Provenance is per token, not per identifier. Three rows, three entry ids, three confidences, and every one of them below 1.0 - a summary field could not carry that.

Four tokens reaching the answer by four different rules in one identifier, each tagged with the rule that fired and the row behind it. This is what makes an audit possible without re-running the resolution.

The reverse direction carries provenance too, and it never reports PINNED or SCORED. REC is a pinned entry, but what settled this answer was the reverse index's tie-break between tokens, not the pin, so claiming PINNED would be false.
